claims.text: Reactive liquid-phase-assisted SPS with a transient sintering aid at about 1700 °C will yield fully dense, single-phase ZrB2.
The resulting ZrB2 will retain strength, oxidation durability, and liquid-metal corrosion resistance comparable to or better than ZrB2 processed above 2300 °C.
ZrB2 synthesized above 2300 °C has an optimal microstructure for strength and oxidation resistance.
ZrB2 processed at about 1700 °C exhibits porosity and microstructural inhomogeneity.
Porosity and microstructural inhomogeneity in lower-temperature ZrB2 cause poor oxidation and liquid-metal corrosion performance.
A transient liquid phase can promote rapid ceramic densification.
The transient liquid phase will produce uniform grain boundaries in ZrB2 at about 1700 °C.
The sintering aid can be completely removed by volatilization or reaction during controlled cooling without leaving secondary phases.
The proposed process is applicable at about 1700 °C under an inert or controlled SPS atmosphere.
The resulting material is intended to withstand oxidation service at or below about 1500 °C.
The resulting material is intended to withstand exposure to liquid plating metals.
Transient liquid-phase sintering will produce near-full density and minimal residual porosity in single-phase ZrB2.
The sintering aid lowers the local melting point and thereby promotes diffusion and densification at reduced bulk temperature.
Removing the aid during cooling leaves a fully densified, homogenized, single-phase microstructure.
Reduced porosity and defect density improve hardness and oxidation resistance.
Reduced porosity and defect density improve stability against corrosion by liquid plating metals.
The treated ZrB2 will have hardness and structural integrity similar or superior to both lower-temperature specimens and high-temperature benchmarks.
The treated ZrB2 will have significantly better oxidation resistance than prior lower-temperature ZrB2.
The treated ZrB2 will have significantly better liquid-plating-metal corrosion resistance than prior lower-temperature ZrB2.
The approach is viable only if the sintering aid can be entirely removed and leaves no performance-degrading residual constituents.

contradictions.description: The intervention and experiment describe controlled cooling as removing or guaranteeing removal of the aid, while the uncertainty field states that complete removal still requires empirical verification.

The predictions and falsification rule require comparison with both lower-temperature specimens and a high-temperature benchmark, but the design permits a control set processed at either condition rather than requiring both control groups.
